title: Acute Mountain Sickness Score -- Definition/Introduction
content: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) is a syndrome that arises in non-acclimatized individuals who ascend to high altitudes. It is a form of acute altitude illness that occurs as the atmospheric partial pressure of oxygen decreases with increasing altitude, inducing hypoxia. This condition typically occurs at altitudes >2500 meters; however, it can occur at lower elevations in high-risk individuals. [1] [2]

title: Acute Mountain Sickness Score -- Clinical Significance
content: AMS can present as a mild self-limiting disease with the presentation of non-specific symptoms such as dizziness, headaches, sleep disturbance, nausea, and vomiting. However, it may also progress to life-threatening complications such as high-altitude pulmonary edema and high-altitude cerebral edema. [3] [4] [5] Hence, early identification of individuals presenting with AMS symptoms can help prevent severe complications. The Lake Louise Questionnaire and the Acute Mountain Sickness-Cerebral score (AMS-C) are 2 assessment tools for identifying AMS.

title: Acute Mountain Sickness Score -- Clinical Significance
content: The AMS-C score is derived from the Environmental Symptom Questionnaire (ESQ), which was developed in 1979 to assess symptoms induced by exposure to extreme environmental conditions. ESQ-III, the third and final revision, consisted of 67 questions, of which 11 are categorized to AMS-C. The questions are scored on a scale of 0 to 5, with 0 indicating “not at all” and 5 indicating “extreme.” Each response score is then multiplied by the factorial weight of its symptom, and a score of 0.70 or greater is classified as AMS-C. Due to ESQ-II being an intricate assessment tool, it is less frequently used. [6] [7]

title: Acute Mountain Sickness Score -- Clinical Significance
content: The Lake Louise Questionnaire was introduced in 1991 and was last modified in 2018.  It is now the most commonly used scoring system to assess AMS. It defines AMS as the presence of headaches, along with 3 other symptoms: gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue/weakness, and dizziness/lightheadedness. Each symptom is assigned a score on a scale from 0 to 3, with 0 indicating no effect and 3 indicating severe. A total score of 3 or greater, with the presence of headaches, in a setting of rapid ascent to high altitude, is diagnosed as AMS. The Lake Louise Questionnaire, although an effective assessment tool, has its limitations. It is a scoring system to standardize and diagnose AMS for use by investigators or research purposes, and it is not meant for clinical practice. [1]

title: Acute Mountain Sickness Score -- Nursing, Allied Health, and Interprofessional Team Interventions
content: Currently, no biomedical tests are available to diagnose AMS; therefore, the disease is diagnosed based on clinical features. The scoring scales serve to identify and assess the presence and intensity of clinical features in an AMS individual. [8] Individuals with a mild presentation of AMS receive treatment with supportive care, including rest, hydration, and analgesic medications. Treatment for more severe cases of AMS includes oxygen and drugs such as acetazolamide or dexamethasone, and descent in altitude. [8] [9] [10]
